name: Battle of Oriskany
info: On 6 August 1777 Loyalists and Britain's Indigenous allies ambushed an American militia column and Oneida warriors under Nicholas Herkimer near Oriska, stopping the relief of Fort Stanwix, though the siege was abandoned two weeks later.

facts.place: A marshy ravine about 6 miles (10 km) east of Fort Stanwix, near the Oneida village of Oriska, in the Mohawk Valley of New York
facts.sides: Tryon County militia, about 800 men, and between 60 and 100 Oneida warriors under Brigadier General Nicholas Herkimer; against a force of roughly 500 under Lieutenant Colonel Sir John Johnson, mostly Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga and Mississauga warriors led by Sayenqueraghta, Cornplanter and Joseph Brant, with Royal Yorkers and Indian Department rangers
facts.outcome: The Americans lost around 465 dead, wounded or captured and Johnson's force 93; the relief column was stopped and Herkimer was mortally wounded, but a sortie from Fort Stanwix looted the warriors' camps and the fighting broke off.

t: The Americans suffered around 465 dead, wounded or captured, against 93 for Johnson's force; about half of Herkimer's men were killed or wounded.
The ambush was sprung too early, and a sortie from Fort Stanwix looted the Indigenous camps, which led the warriors to break off the fight to protect their women and possessions.
The battle began a civil war among the Haudenosaunee, as Oneida and Tuscarora warriors sided with the Patriots and the Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga with the Loyalist cause.
dyk: Many of the men who fought each other at Oriskany had been neighbours, and the Royal Yorkers' ruse of turning their coats inside out to pass as a relief party from the fort failed when a Patriot captain recognised a Loyalist neighbour.
ev: Britain launches a two-pronged attack from Quebec, with Burgoyne coming down Lake Champlain and St. Leger down the Mohawk Valley
Herkimer issues a proclamation warning of British activity and calls out the Tryon County militia after Oneida allies report the British close to Fort Stanwix
St. Leger besieges Fort Stanwix and Herkimer's column sets out from Fort Dayton and camps near Oriska
Johnson's force ambushes Herkimer's column in a ravine near Oriska
A sortie from Fort Stanwix under Marinus Willett raids the Indigenous and Loyalist camps, and the warriors break off the fighting
Herkimer dies on 16 August of his wounds
Benedict Arnold's relief column reaches Fort Stanwix and the besiegers withdraw
John Butler is authorised to raise Butler's Rangers, with Indian Department rangers from Oriskany as its core

sections.background:
In June 1777 the British Army launched a two-pronged attack from Quebec. General John Burgoyne's objective was to split New England from the other colonies by gaining control of New York's Hudson Valley. The main thrust came south across Lake Champlain under Burgoyne; the second, led by Brigadier General Barry St. Leger, was meant to come down the Mohawk Valley and meet Burgoyne's army near Albany.

St. Leger's expedition numbered about 1,800 men: British regulars, Creuzbourg's Jäger Corps, Loyalists from the Royal Yorkers and the British Indian Department, and Indigenous warriors of several nations, including the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, Mohawk and Mississauga. The main body travelled from Lachine up the Saint Lawrence and along the shore of Lake Ontario to the Oswego River. There it was joined by British Indian Department rangers from Fort Niagara under Deputy Superintendent John Butler and several hundred Indigenous warriors. The expedition crossed Oneida Lake to the Oneida Carry, and Fort Stanwix, a Continental Army outpost at the east end of the portage, was besieged from 2 August.

In the valley, Nicholas Herkimer, head of Tryon County's Committee of Safety, had been warned of a possible British attack along the Mohawk River. On 17 July he issued a proclamation warning of military activity and urging the people to respond if needed. On 30 July Oneida allies told him that the British were four days from Fort Stanwix, and he put out a call to arms.
sections.forces:
The relief column was drawn from the Tryon County militia, about 800 men, poorly trained farmers who were chiefly of Palatine German descent. It set out from Fort Dayton on 4 August and camped near the Oneida village of Oriska on 5 August. A number of the militia dropped out because of their lack of conditioning, but the column was joined by a company of 60 to 100 Oneida warriors led by Han Yerry, a strong supporter of the Patriot cause. That evening Herkimer sent three men to Colonel Peter Gansevoort, the fort's commander, who was to signal receipt of the message with three cannon shots and then sortie to meet the column. The couriers had difficulty getting through the British lines and did not deliver it until late the next morning, after the battle was under way.

St. Leger learned on 5 August that the column was coming, from a message Molly Brant sent to her brother Joseph Brant, the Mohawk leader of part of St. Leger's Indigenous contingent. He sent Royal Yorkers light infantry towards Oriska that evening, and Brant and Butler followed early the next morning with about 400 Indigenous warriors and Indian Department rangers. Many of the warriors had muskets; others carried only tomahawks and spears. The force under Lieutenant Colonel Sir John Johnson is put at roughly 500 men, most of them Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga and Mississauga warriors led by Sayenqueraghta, Cornplanter and Brant. The Seneca chiefs Sayenqueraghta and Cornplanter chose the ground for an ambush: a marshy ravine, where the Royal Yorkers were to stop the head of the column and the Haudenosaunee on both sides would attack the extended column.
sections.course:
Herkimer held a war council on the morning of 6 August. He wanted to wait because he had not heard the expected signal from the fort, but his captains pressed him to go on, accusing him of being a Tory because his brother was serving under St. Leger. Stung by this, he ordered the column to march. At about 10 am the column descended into the ravine, crossed the stream and began to climb the far side, Herkimer on horseback near the front.

Contrary to the plan, the warriors opened fire too early, but the Patriots were taken completely by surprise. Colonel Ebenezer Cox was shot from his horse and killed in the first volley, and a ball shattered Herkimer's leg and killed his horse. He was carried to a beech tree, where he sat smoking a pipe and giving directions. Part of the column had not yet entered the ravine; most of those men panicked and fled, and some attackers pursued them. Thirty minutes in, only about half of Herkimer's men were still fighting.

The militia rallied and fought its way to the crest on the west side. A thunderstorm paused the fighting for an hour. When it resumed, Royal Yorkers turned their coats inside out to pass as a relief party from the fort, but Captain Jacob Gardinier recognised a Loyalist neighbour. Close combat followed, often between former neighbours. Herkimer's messengers reached the fort around 11 a.m., and Lieutenant Colonel Marinus Willett led 250 men out to raid the nearly deserted camps to the south. A warrior ran to the field with the news, and the Haudenosaunee, giving the Seneca signal to retire, left to protect their women and possessions, which forced the smaller number of German and Loyalist fighters to withdraw.
sections.aftermath:
The Americans lost around 465 dead, wounded or captured, and Johnson's force 93 killed, wounded or captured. About half of Herkimer's force were killed or wounded, as were about 15 percent of the Loyalist force. The Indigenous warriors retrieved most of their dead by the following day, but many dead and wounded Patriots were left on the field. Herkimer was carried off and his leg amputated, but the operation went poorly and he died on 16 August. The battered remnant retreated to Fort Dayton.

The sortie had cost the warriors their possessions, which damaged their morale and contributed to the failure of St. Leger's expedition. Brant and Sayenqueraghta proposed pursuing the Patriots downriver towards German Flatts, but St. Leger turned them down. General Philip Schuyler organised more relief, and Benedict Arnold's column reached Fort Stanwix on 21 August. His messengers convinced the besiegers that his force was much larger than it was, and they abandoned the siege. Arnold's men, marching through weeks after the battle, were moved by the stench and grisly scene.

The battle was the first time the Haudenosaunee had fought one another. The Haudenosaunee in St. Leger's camp met in council and sent the Patriot-allied Oneidas a bloody hatchet. Brant's Mohawks burned the Oneida settlement of Oriska, and the Oneidas plundered the Mohawk strongholds of Tiononderoge and Canajoharie, and later raided the Fort Hunter Mohawks, so that most of the remaining Mohawks in central New York fled to Quebec.
sections.sources:
Among the accounts of the battle is that of Dr. Moses Younglove, a Patriot prisoner, who accused the British and Loyalists of aiding and abetting the murders of prisoners and claimed that Indigenous warriors ate two of them. The Canadian historian Gavin Watt has described his account as "highly coloured" and "extremely suspect". Many captives were turned over to the British, while some were tortured and killed.

Governor Blacksnake, in an interview many years afterwards, recalled that he "thought at that time the Blood Shed a Stream running down on the decending [sic] ground", and Haudenosaunee oral histories know the place as "A Place of Great Sadness". The casualty figures stand at around 465 Americans and 93 on Johnson's side, the first described as dead, wounded or captured. Historians weigh who gained most: the battle may be considered a success for St. Leger because he stopped the relief column, yet news of the sortie may have averted the complete destruction of Herkimer's force, which remained on the field after the Loyalist withdrawal.
sections.legacy:
The battle was one of the bloodiest of the war by the share of casualties suffered, and it was one of the few in which most non-Indigenous participants were settlers born in the Thirteen Colonies. The British success was tempered by discontent among their Indigenous allies. When they joined the expedition they expected British forces to do most of the fighting, but they were the dominant fighters at Oriskany, and the loss of their belongings in the sortie was a blow to their morale that contributed to the failure of St. Leger's expedition.

The battle marked the beginning of a civil war among the Haudenosaunee, as Oneida warriors under Louis Cook and Han Yerry aligned with the Patriot cause, as did the Tuscarora, while the Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga were allied to the Loyalist cause. In September 1777 Butler was authorised to raise a Loyalist unit that became Butler's Rangers, with Indian Department rangers who had fought at Oriskany as its core.

A monument was erected in 1883, and much of the battlefield is preserved in the Oriskany Battlefield State Historic Site. The site was recognised as a National Historic Landmark in 1962 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1966. The town and county of Herkimer, New York, were named in Herkimer's honour, and the battle gave its name to the aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, launched in 1945, and to a postage stamp issued in 1977.

summary: At Oriskany on 6 August 1777 Loyalists and Haudenosaunee warriors allied to Britain ambushed a Tryon County militia column and its Oneida allies under Nicholas Herkimer, who was mortally wounded. About half his force was killed or wounded, and the battle began a civil war among the Haudenosaunee.
references: Richard Berleth, Bloody Mohawk: the French and Indian War & American Revolution on New York's Frontier (Black Dome Press, 2009)
notes: The article gives Johnson's force as roughly 500 men and Brant and Butler's party as about 400 warriors and rangers; both are given with their attribution and not reconciled.
The article says the Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots in one place and that 'some Oneidas' were allied with the British in another; I kept to the first.
Article text 'Leger' without St. appears once in the lead; I wrote St. Leger throughout.
'Oneida village of Oriska' is also the settlement Brant's Mohawks burned 'later in the siege'.
The article gives the Americans' 465 as 'dead, wounded, or captured', with no breakdown; the 93 likewise.

Left out: Louis Cook's shot at a warrior, Johnson's return to camp for 70 men, Herkimer's order to fight in pairs, the ravine's measurements, Willett's four prisoners and the seizure of Johnson's papers, for length.
The article does not say Governor Blacksnake fought at the battle; the text only says he recalled it in an interview.
